chapter_learning_objectives: Identify family roles, structure, and functions
Identify various factors that can lead to actual and potential family health problems
Compare and contrast parenting styles and behaviors
Consider the influence of family cultural practices related to health
Identify the psychosocial effect of illness on a client and their family's health
Apply the nursing process to caring for a client in the context of the family

sections.title: Introduction
facts: Family dynamics affect health, illness, and recovery outcomes
Plan of care considers family roles, cultural practices, psychosocial impact of chronic disease/disability on family functioning
For pediatric clients: assess parenting styles/behaviors, provide anticipatory guidance
Health teaching includes family while respecting client confidentiality and privacy

sections.title: Family Structures, Cultural Practices, Roles, and Functions
facts: Family (US Census): two or more people, one the householder, related by birth, marriage, or adoption, residing together
Family of orientation = family grew up in; family of procreation = family formed as adult
Family developmental stages: independence → coupling/marriage → parenting → launching adult children → retirement/senior years
Culture: shared values, norms, symbols, language, objects, way of life passed between generations
ANA standard 'Respectful and Equitable Practice' = cultural humility + inclusiveness
Implicit bias: unconscious negative attitude toward a social group; shaped by experience; can affect nursing care
Family roles: recurrent behavior patterns fulfilling family functions; expand/change over life; impaired by chronic illness
Informal roles: decision-maker (culturally determined, may vary by decision type), peace-maker, tradition-holder
Unhealthy roles in dysfunction: golden child, hero, mascot, identified patient/scapegoat, invisible child, lost child, enabler/caretaker, parentified child
Five family functions: economic support, emotional support, socialization, control of sexuality/reproduction, ascribed social status
Intimacy = mutually shared trust; buffers external stressors
Socialization: family as first teacher of norms, values, emotional display rules; can also transmit unhealthy behaviors
Ascribed status (at birth) vs achieved status (by effort); family support affects achievement

sections.title: Family Dynamics
facts: Family dynamics: roles, relationships, communication patterns, factors shaping interactions
Healthy relationships = security/comfort; unhealthy = stress (arguments, intrusion, criticism)
Families can be functional in some characteristics and dysfunctional in others simultaneously
High-resource families: resiliency + resources (financial, extended family, friends, faith community)
Low-resource families: do not effectively meet members' needs
Family dysfunction = failure of the five family functions; usually unintended; transmitted across generations
Caregiver trauma affects child's sense of self, communication, relationships, future health

sections.title: Factors That Lead to Actual and Potential Family Health Problems
facts: ACE: neglect (physical/emotional), abuse (physical/emotional/sexual), divorce, family member imprisonment, witnessing substance abuse/mental illness, witnessing parent treated violently

ACE Study (late 1990s, >17,000 participants): dose-response — more ACE → more adolescent risk behavior, adult chronic illness (alcoholism, COPD, depression, liver disease); highest ACE → 20-year lower life expectancy

Family risk factors for ACE: special-needs caregiving, limited understanding of child development, caregiver abused as child, young caregivers, single parents, low income/education, financial stress, inconsistent discipline/spanking, low supervision, isolation, high conflict, attitudes accepting violence
Community risk factors: violence/crime, limited opportunity, poverty/unemployment/food insecurity, drug/alcohol access, low involvement, few youth activities, unstable housing

Family protective factors: basic needs met, stable secure nurturing relationships, social support, positive shared activities, school valued, peaceful conflict resolution, outside mentors, caregiver education/employment, effective supervision/discipline, problem-solving help

Community protective factors: parenting education, financial assistance, medical/mental health services, safe housing, safe childcare, quality preschool, after-school programs, family-friendly employment
Divorce is an ACE; effect moderated by how parents treat each other before/during/after

Divorce guidance for parents: never force sides, no arguments/criticism in front of child, talk early and often, allow child to share fears; be honest in simple terms, child not at fault, reassure love, be patient with questions
Maintain routine, friends, school, environment; consistent rules across households; keep promises
Inform teachers/counselors so problems at school are reported

sections.title: Parenting Styles and Behaviors
facts: Psychosocial development: intersection of social, cultural, environmental influences on mind and behavior
Parenting: nurturing, caring for, socializing, preparing children for adult roles; child response, genetics, peers also influence
Two axes: parental responsiveness (warmth/support) × parental demandingness (behavioral control)
Four styles: uninvolved (low/low), permissive (high warmth/low control), authoritarian (low warmth/high control), authoritative (high/high)
Third dimension: psychological control (guilt, love withdrawal, shaming); authoritarian expects unquestioned compliance, authoritative explains rationale

Outcomes: uninvolved → poor in all domains; permissive → behavior problems, lower academics, but higher self-esteem/social skills; authoritarian → moderate academics, poorer social skills, lower self-esteem, more depression; authoritative → best across domains incl. lowest underage drinking risk
Positive parenting behaviors: good communication, effective discipline, socialization, teaching responsibility
Good communication: active listening, eye contact, screens off, scheduled connection, validate feelings, read/talk to infants; avoid commanding, lecturing, ridiculing
Communication patterns: 'I' language; focus on behavior not personality; focus on solution not person; model calm and manners; attend to good behavior
Discipline = guidance, not punishment; age-appropriate
Time-out: 1 minute per year of age; follow with hug, positive words, reinforcement
Spanking: not effective; teaches hitting to get what you want
Older children: short-term privilege removal; then restate rule, positive attention, reinforce
Consequence steps: clear guidelines + warning → specific if-then consequence fitting behavior → immediate follow-through → positive reinforcement after
Behaviorism: attend to desired behavior, ignore undesired if child is safe (e.g., tantrum); afterwards name the emotion and teach acceptable expression
Without intentional positive attention, child may act out — any attention beats none
Socialization: name the behavior not the child; specific praise not vague 'good job'; model empathy; balanced self-esteem / growth mindset

Responsibility: developmentally matched chores; specific instructions (what/when/how), supervise, praise/small rewards (sticker chart), consequence only if repeated non-completion; rewards more effective than consequences
Parental traits: warm, conscientious, agreeable, low-anxiety caregivers support autonomy; developmental history repeats or is deliberately changed
Bidirectional: child temperament, birth order, health status shape parent behavior; challenging children → more punitive parents over time
Parenting characteristics driven by parent's psychological needs: martyr, pal, police officer/drill sergeant, expert, coach
Sociocultural: financial hardship, cultural values (autonomy vs group harmony), dangerous neighborhood → less warmth, more restriction (adaptive)

sections.title: Psychosocial Effect of Illness on Client and Family Health
facts: One member's illness affects the family: parents manage regimens/appointments/finances; siblings may feel unvalued, adopt lost-child role; SUD in family → enabling, ignoring, financial drain
Family caregivers: regular care for chronic illness/disability — ADLs, bills, shopping, transport, emotional support; strain rises as needs rise
Caregiver role strain: difficulty performing the caregiver role
US: 22% of adults provided care in past 30 days; 10% to someone with dementia/cognitive impairment; ~25% of dementia caregivers are sandwich-generation
Caregiving can enhance quality of life but also impair work, social life, physical and mental health

Caregiver stress signs to monitor: anger/frustration, social withdrawal, anxiety about future, depression/decreased coping, exhaustion, sleeplessness, irritability/poor concentration, emerging health problems
Community resources: child/adult day care, respite care (home volunteer/paid), residential facility, palliative care

Caregiver self-care teaching: provider visits, nutrition, exercise, rest; relaxation breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, visualization, meditation; 'taking care of yourself helps you be a better caregiver'
Family-centered care: client-centered approach emphasizing family involvement/collaboration in care and decisions
FCC benefits: better outcomes, less family stress/anxiety, better family-provider relationships, higher satisfaction, better resource use
FCC principles: respect and dignity; collaboration; empowerment; information sharing
Family therapy targets relationship/interaction patterns; refer when SUD affects family
Support groups: Al-Anon, Nar-Anon (family SUD); Sibshop (siblings of children with disabilities)

sections.title: Applying the Nursing Process and Clinical Judgment Model
facts: ASSESSMENT / RECOGNIZE CUES: establish cultural safety and privacy first; open-ended cultural question; identify decision-maker (parent/guardian <18, POA, cultural elder) while advocating autonomy
Ask client privately who they want present; nurse asks others to leave if client prefers — client may not feel empowered to

General survey of client AND family: hygiene, affect/mood, communication, nutrition, fluid status → signs of neglect, abuse, substance misuse; observe roles, relationships, interaction patterns, emotional support

Healthy cue: mutual respect, trust, caring communication. Unhealthy cue: unfriendly, disrespectful, hostile → notify provider, refer social work/case management per policy; suspected abuse → state mandated reporting + agency policy
Family effect questions: what family knows about illness; how family responds (overprotective/frustrated/anxious); awareness of support groups, respite, community resources
Cultural Formulation Interview (APA) family items: supports that help; stresses that worsen; background/identity aspects that matter; help others have suggested
DIAGNOSIS / ANALYZE CUES: NANDA diagnoses related to family processes, parenting, caregiving (Table 4.7); use current evidence-based care-planning resource

OUTCOME IDENTIFICATION / GENERATE SOLUTIONS: collaborative goals with client and family per values/culture; sample goals — effective coping and support systems; meet member needs or seek help; identify risks; focus on wellness/prevention; balance exercise/work/leisure/rest/nutrition
SMART outcome examples: after teaching, family describes three healthy coping strategies; parent describes available supports; parent describes three home safety risks
IMPLEMENTATION / TAKE ACTION: reprioritize against current condition; focused assessments — understanding of condition and needs, economic resources/social support, ACE, strengths/weaknesses

Interventions: rapport; recognize formal/informal decision roles; acknowledge emotions; encourage expression; encourage visits/participation (with adult client permission); strength-oriented psychoeducation; spiritual support; caregiver skill-building; mobilize social support; refer family therapy/resources; model communication and regulation; involve family in discharge planning
EVALUATION / EVALUATE OUTCOMES: was diagnosis accurate/complete; goals met per timeline or progressing; keep/modify/delete diagnoses, goals, outcomes, interventions; need more data?

sections.title: Spotlight Application
sections.license_note: CC BY 4.0 — this worked case IS usable, unlike the 4.9 case study

case.situation: 8-year-old with abdominal pain; mother present; parents divorcing
assessment: pain assessment (onset, location, duration, character, aggravating/relieving, treatment)
dynamics: respect, communication, nurturing, protection; needs met?
child's feelings about divorce; sense of responsibility
case.goal: family works cooperatively to provide support for the child
case.smart_outcome: by end of teaching session, parent describes three ways to mitigate effects of divorce for the child
interventions: teach child divorce is not their fault
recommend community resources for divorcing families
evaluation: child verbalizes understanding of divorce and living arrangements?
parents report ability to support child's emotional health?
case.next_step: document progress toward goal; SMART outcome met/partially/not met; set reevaluation time

legacy_crosswalk.legacy_chapter: NCC Unit 1 Ch.1 Family-Centered Nursing Care (ATI-aligned, no source text)
legacy_crosswalk.coverage: Every legacy slide topic (family structure/function, parenting/discipline, assessment cues, priority risks, nursing actions, teaching, communication, safety/policy, interprofessional, case, evaluation, documentation) has a corresponding SRC01 section. Legacy S04 'Parenting + Discipline' → 4.5; S05 'Assessment Cues' → 4.7 recognize cues; S06 'Priority Risks' → 4.4 ACE; S07 'Nursing Actions' → 4.7 take action; S09 'Therapeutic Communication' → 4.5 communication patterns + 4.7; S10 'Safety + Policy' → 4.7 mandated reporting; S11 'Interprofessional' → 4.6 resources; S12 case → 4.8 spotlight.
legacy_crosswalk.implication: The legacy chapter can be re-grounded on SRC01 without changing its structure. Chapter 4 also supplies what legacy lacked: an organizing question candidate (4.1), explicit CJM mapping (4.7), and a CC BY worked case (4.8).
